subsubtopic: FOOD AID NOT ANSWER TO WORLD HUNGER
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the western Premiers recommended that Canada reduce its growing stockpiles of grain by sending the surplus to feed the hungry peoples of our world.
It hurts the food producers of western Canada to see the food they have grown going to waste while other people in the world go hungry. In our world half a billion people live in a state of constant hunger and 40 million people, half of them children, die of hunger every year.
In spite of the humanitarian desire to share our surplus with Third World peoples, we need to realize that food aid does not provide the answer to world hunger. Except in cases of extreme emergency, food aid can do more harm than good by distorting the price paid for food and destroying the incentive for local agriculture.
Canada already provides a very large percentage of its development assistance in the form of food aid, larger than that of any other nation. CIDA is already a major customer of the Canadian Wheat Board.
The solution to Canada's agricultural problems is urgently needed but this solution cannot be found in a proposal that destroys food production in Africa, Asia or South America. These nations need development assistance, not food aid.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO VOLUNTEERS WHO WORK FOR LAC-SAINT-JEAN REGIONAL CYSTIC FIBROSIS ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Last Saturday, May 23, Mr. Speaker, Alma in my riding was the site of a rocking chair endurance contest sponsored by the Lac-Saint-Jean Regional Cystic Fibrosis Association.
I was glad to join the "rockers" and make my modest contribution to help finance research which gives every child victim a ray of hope for the future.
I would be remiss if I failed to mention the participation of Mrs. Diane Hebert who epitomizes genuine determination and whose presence was undoubtedly a major factor behind the outstanding success of this event which proved rewarding beyond expectations.
I conclude by emphasizing the good work accomplished by all volunteers who have been actively supporting this association for a number of years.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF PATENT ACT AMENDMENTS-PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my opposition to and anger at the comments made by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with regard to the effects of Bill C-22. In a recent speech in Montreal, the Prime Minister misled the people of Quebec by indicating to them that there would be untold benefits as a result of the passage of Bill C-22. What the Prime Minister failed to say is what benefits will be bestowed upon the people of Manitoba. Particularly, will those in Brandon, Manitoba, see any benefits for research and development as a result of Bill C-22? Will Nova Scotians receive any benefits for research and technology as a result of Bill C-22? The answer is an unequivocal no.
The benefits of Bill C-22 will not be distributed across Canada in an equitable way. The people of Canada are once again being hosed by a Government that wishes to cater to the

May 27, 1987
multinational corporations centered in New York, Philadelphia and elsewhere. I call upon the Government to change this most regressive piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is with regret that this House records the recent death of Air Marshal Hugh Campbell, former Chief of Air Staff and a man of long and distinguished service in the Canadian military who did much to develop the Royal Canadian Air Force.
Air Marshal Campbell earned his wings at Camp Borden in 1930, and served in the United Kingdom and the Middle East during World War II, rising to the rank of Air Vice Marshal when appointed to the Air Council. After the War, he was much involved with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
In northern Canada, Hugh Campbell will be remembered as an appointed Member of the Northwest Territories Council who worked himself out of a job as he promoted elected and democratic government for northerners. We extend our thanks for a lifetime of service, and our condolences to family and friends.

subsubtopic: PHONEY REFUGEE CLAIMANTS FROM PORTUGAL-DELAY IN INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Tory Government shields rich, powerful crooks by attacking the poor and weak. Two years ago immigration officials knew that crooks were bringing phoney refugee claimants from Portugal by means of the "persecuted Jehovah's Witness scam". Not until January, 1986, did the RCMP investigate and not until July, 1986, after thousands of duped Portuguese paid thousands of dollars each to crooks, did the Government impose a visa requirement on Portuguese visitors.
At that time the Hon. Minister promised, privately to me and publicly: "We're going to lay charges and we're going to make them stick, if I have to hire the lawyers myself." One year later, no RCMP investigators have gone to Lisbon and no charges have been laid. The Government has rewarded rich crooks by stalling the investigation.
But to cover up this shameful action, the Government attacks real refugees. Men, women and children fleeing brutal police states in Chile and El Salvador are called "liars, phoneys" and "economic migrants" so as to shield the rich crooks. What a disgrace to Canada this Tory Government is.

subsubtopic: EXPROPRIATED PEOPLE OF MIRABEL-DESIRE THAT SURPLUS LAND IN 8,000 ACRE BUFFER ZONE BE RESTORED TO ORIGINAL OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever mindful of its commitments, our Government signed a draft agreement with Mirabel's expropriated people on March 25, 1985, a historic date. Since then the land resale process has been going on as expected, and today I fully support and endorse the expropriated owners' request that the Montreal International Airport North Terminal buffer zone be reduced to 8,000 acres and the surplus land be restored to the original owners.
Mr. Speaker, whereas the 8,000 acres are more than enough to meet current and future needs of the airport over the next 50 years; whereas this surplus land was needlessly expropriated, thus playing havoc with the lives of hundreds of families and uprooting entire villages; and whereas the expropriation deprived Quebec and Mirabel residents of a major agricultural output, I earnestly hope, Mr. Speaker, that the surplus land of this 8,000-acre buffer zone will be resold at the earliest opportunity.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S DECISION TO CUT BENEFITS TO OLDER WORKERS
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, I rise to commemorate the passing of Canada's quintessential King of joie de vivre within the sporting world. Paul Rimstead, renowned newspaper columnist and television personality, died in Florida yesterday.
A long-time resident in my constituency, Paul won the respect of fellow writers and the people he wrote about. His years with the now defunct Canadian magazine, The Toronto Telegram and The Toronto Sun proved he could always get the story behind the story. Paul had that special quality in a writer-he built his interviews on a foundation of trust. His eccentric lifestyle was a matter of public record, and his energy often the envy of his peers.
Paul is survived by his wife, his mother, five sisters, a brother and a daughter. He will long be remembered for his ability to make ordinary people larger than life and make common events veritable Superbowls. Paul Rimstead has come and gone in the tradition of a true Canadian newspaperman, and his insights will be missed among the morning news.

subsubtopic: SHORTAGE OF DECENT HOUSING-NEED TO ADDRESS SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless. In Canada, despite our wealth, between 20,000 and 30,000 people are without a place to sleep at night. Yet CMHC, the federal agency charged with housing policy, estimates it accounts for only 1 per cent of total federal government expenditures. It is obvious the Government's commitment is totally inadequate.
In addition to those who must resort to sleeping in public places and those who find shelter on a short-term basis with churches and other charitable organizations, we must be aware of the hidden homeless in Canada. Because of high housing costs and the shortage of decent housing, many people, for example young couples, are forced to share living accommodation with parents, relatives and others.
We need imaginative policies and an increase in resources to meet the challenge of decent and adequate housing for all Canadians. The federal Government, through CMHC, should take the responsibility and address the crisis. I call upon the Minister to show the political will to deal realistically with this shameful situation.

Mr. Speaker, the Laurentian region will be advertised throughout the world, thanks to an extensive industrial promotion campaign launched recently by members from the region, together with the regional industrial commissioners and the Corporation de developpement des Laurentides.
This campaign, launched under the theme Laurentides Plus, with the slogan: More than an environment, an industrial site, will make our region better known, not only in Canada but also abroad where there are major markets for our goods.
The campaign includes a Laurentides Plus poster, which will be sent to more than 50 Canadian embassies, high commissioners' offices and consulates throughout the world.
I am convinced that the Government's assistance will have a major impact on the economy of the Laurentian region.

subsubtopic: MEETING OF CANADIAN PARLIAMENTARY ASSOCIATION AT QUEBEC CITY-IMPACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Canadian NATO Parliamentary Association, I had the honour last week-end to be a Canadian delegate to the spring session which took place in the lovely city of Quebec.
In the course of discussions at the Economic Commission on May 22, 1987, Professor Rodrigue Tremblay of the University of Montreal made a speech, which I found very apt, relating to international trade negotiations in which Canada is an active participant.
In discussing free trade, Professor Tremblay pointed out that Canada and the United States were setting an example to countries presently negotiating the Uruguay Round of multilateral trade agreements. The Canada-U.S. talks have shown that economic barriers between countries can be abolished, as they were in Europe in 1958.
The spring NATO session, the discussions on the economy and the responsibilities of Canadian delegates within the various commissions all reminded me, Mr. Speaker, of the major role that Canada can play on the international scene.
By taking the initiative for the Canada-U.S. talks and by taking an active part in the new Uruguay Round of multilateral trade negotiations, our Government has shown the kind of priority it sets on reducing trade barriers and its concern for giving Canadians better opportunities for selling their products on international markets.

May 27, 1987

subtopic: USE OF COCAINE-GOVERNMENT'S ACTION ON DRUG ABUSE CAMPAIGN WELCOMED
USE OF COCAINE-GOVERNMENT'S ACTION ON DRUG ABUSE CAMPAIGN WELCOMED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a parent 1 would like to commend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for initiating his campaign against drug abuse. The critics say there is no crisis but I think the fact that over 200,000 Canadians were using cocaine in 1985 more than proves that something needs to be done about drug abuse in our country. The Government's five-year $210 million program emphasizes public education, research, and rehabilitation. I think it will certainly help some people who now have addictions and will help prevent others from becoming drug abusers.
Those of us who are blessed with the opportunity and responsibility of being parents recognize all too often how ill-prepared we are for some of the challenges which parenting presents. The worry that a family member may become addicted to drugs or alcohol is one of the most fearsome challenges facing parents today.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, the public education aspect of this program will be extremely valuable in helping parents and educators put across the message that using drugs is not "cool". The program will also be a big help to families of drug abusers who fear that their love alone may not be enough to help someone with a serious drug problem, a problem with which they have neither experience nor understanding.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. This morning the Premiers at the Western Premiers Conference issued a communique calling on the Government of Canada to make an early announcement of an increased and substantial deficiency payment to western farmers due to declining prices and income. Yesterday the Prime Minister told the House that we should not be recommending exactly the kind of thing that the western Premiers are calling for.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend knows that the Government has stood behind the western farmers. We have in the past, and we will again in the future. We recognize the contribution of the agricultural community to the well-being of the nation and I have indicated on many occasions that we clearly established our bona fides in this regard. This Government understands the problems and the commitment of farmers and shall stand behind farmers.
I also indicated yesterday that there was a very important international dimension to the problem, which dealt with the crippling trade subsidy war in agricultural subsidies between the European Community and the United States of America. This is very much a debilitating problem for Canadian farmers because this kind of highly subsidized traffic is in the process of artificially taking part and parcel of traditional Canadian markets unfairly.
It is this particular practice which, if allowed to extend, could fatally wound free traders in agriculture like Canada. That is why at the Cairns Group, at the OECD and at the Summit, we have elevated agriculture and the very significant real problems of agricultural subsidies to an international forum so that we can hopefully bring a degree of sanity to this very grave problem of agricultural subsidies. If it is not solved, the Canadian farmer will pay an unfair price. We must make sure that the farmer is not called upon to pay that kind of unfair price.

Mr. Speaker, President Fanfani of Italy is reported to have told the Prime Minister that the grain trade wars would probably not even be on the agenda of the Venice Summit in June. How can the Prime
May 27, 1987

Minister raise expectations that he can solve this problem for our grain farmers, which will put thousands of them off the farms this year, if it is not even on the agenda of the Summit?

First, Mr. Speaker, the statement attributed to the President of the Council, Mr. Fanfani, is false. There was no such statement made.
In fact, I, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the Minister of Finance, repeatedly with him and others, yesterday raised the question that it is the resolve of Canada to make sure that agriculture and agricultural subsidies were very much dealt with at the Summit. We did it in Tokyo and we will do it again in Venice. That is very much in keeping with the international posture of this nation, to recognize that there is a domestic component to the problem and a solution, but without an international solution the problem will persist. That is why it is so important that we be vigilant at the international fora which is precisely the area where Canada is providing the leadership which must come on behalf of Canadian farmers.

consistent with every single action this Government has taken, namely, that we must rid ourselves of these artificial subsidies because, in the long run, they cripple Canadian farmers by depriving Canadian farmers, who are fair traders, of a fair share of world markets.

I should say we are certainly pleased that Premier Devine is going to raise the matter with the French President. However, we are more interested in what the Canadian Government is going to do. Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend was a member of the Ministry-and he is from western Canada-which in 1984-85 provided federal assistance to grain and oilseed producers of $1,185 billion. This Government has provided to the same farmers an amount of $3,750 billion. That is a 350 per cent increase in terms of aid to western agriculture.
Hear, hear!
Are the farmers better off?
There is the Newfoundland farmer being heard from.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Right Hon. Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I think my answers yesterday and in other circumstances indicate very clearly that we are doing what a responsible national Government must do, which is to fight this at both levels, namely, provide the farmers with required domestic support, which is incontrovertible-the figures indicate an increase of some 350 per cent of federal assistance to western farmers from the time we were sworn in, approximately-second, a very vigorous international program at the OECD with the Cairns Group, with the Summit leaders, to ensure that the ultimate solution is one which benefits Canadian farmers.
Canadian farmers know better than most people in this House of Commons, and most bureaucrats, the international dimension of the problem. They know full well that the

May 27, 1987
Oral Questions
international commodity pricing problem was not created on the floor of this House of Commons and that it requires an international solution. They approve the initiatives of this Government to bring about an international solution to a problem which is crippling their growth.
Mr. Speaker, I simply want to point out to the Prime Minister that in his answers he forgot a couple of important facts.
Question.

He forgot that in 1984 the average price of grain was $170 a tonne, not $110 as it is now. In 1984, 30 per cent of Canadian farmers were not facing bankruptcy. That is the difference between now and then.

I want to ask the Prime Minister the question again. No one argues at all with the need to find an international solution, but what about the domestic solution, not a domestic solution in the past, a domestic solution now? Is the Prime Minister once again saying that he is refusing to respond to the western Premiers and the western farmers and will not provide a deficiency payment? Or will he say today that he will provide the solution wanted by western farmers and keep them in business for the forthcoming crop year?

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised at the question. The answer is clearly in the action that we have taken, as well as in the responses to questions asked yesterday on this specific point in which we indicated that, on the one hand, we are very directly involved in assisting western farmers at this particular point in time while, on the other hand, we are very desirous of working internationally to bring about a solution.
Two weeks ago I had meetings with leading members of farm groups and farmers in western Canada. A few days ago with the Minister for International Trade, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Deputy Prime Minister, and the Minister of Agriculture, I met with leaders of the Cairns Group with regard to the international dimension. On Friday, in just a few days, I will meet again with western agricultural leaders here in Ottawa to refine our national strategy in regard to the presentations at the Summit.
Apart from assistance nationally, and a complex, but we think effective, program internationally, there is also a fundamental other ingredient which has to enter this mix. It is attitudinal. It has to deal with our desire to help farmers and family farms.
With respect to the contrast in attitudes, I ask my hon. friend from western Canada to consider this. When the call came to this Government to assist western farmers we said: "Yes". When it came in the past the response from someone
else was: "Why should I sell your wheat?" That is the difference.
Hear, hear!

I believe 1 and other Members of this House, particularly those in the Opposition but also government back-benchers, have to be sure the information we take from this House or committee is a clear reflection of why the Government makes a decision and what that decision is. If a Member is provided with two different versions or interpretations by the same Minister on the same day, then I believe that individual's ability to function as a Member of Parliament is somewhat compromised; in this case, perhaps my privilege has been violated.
1 would like to read to you two short excerpts from the Standing Committee on Transport and the House last Thursday. This is the nub of my concern. Reading first from the committee, and to give you the context I will start with the question 1 put to the Minister:
Do you have any indication whatsoever that the increase in the price per car- or to what extent the increase in the price per car-was due to design changes after the initial proposal was sent by VIA to the consortium?

No, I do not. I do not have that information. It has been suggested that there was a premium because this Trans Consortium was formed. You know that there might have been a saving if the tenders had been called and they were both bidding against one and another. And that is possible that there was a cost premium there, but 1 do not have any figure for what you are discussing there.

Your department has not analysed the bid and the negotiated agreement as it relates to the-because I mean you yourself have said we are not doing it because we cannot afford it. The price is higher than we anticipated.

Well, as I understand, there is a certain price tender per car which was too much and that price was substantially reduced after a series of discussions and negotiation. So the consortium reduced the price some hundreds of thousands of dollars per car as a result of discussions and negotiations after their original price was put in. But it still left it well in excess of three million dollars per car.

Just a final question. Mr. Minister, would you conclude then, that the final price per car was realistic, separate from the issue whether the money was available, but that the Government and VIA were not getting taken to the cleaners by the Trans Consortium because of a lack of competition?
Here is the key element in the Minister's response:

I do not think Trans Consortium were attempting to take anyone to the cleaners. Naturally if you are bidding against one and another you are going to do everything you can to be competitive and shave prices. So probably the effect of inviting them both to work and tender together on it would result in a higher cost, but 1 do not think they were attempting to take anyone to the cleaners.
Later that day in the House, in response to my question, the Minister said:
The hon. gentleman should ask the companies which he mentioned whether they were keeping that problem in mind when they submitted their prices to do
May 27, 1987

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (for the Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-57, an Act to amend the Export and Import Permits Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, on April 8, I announced the Government's intention to introduce an amendment to the Export and Import Permits Act to permit the monitoring of all steel exports and imports. Members will recall the importance I placed then on maintaining open access to the U.S. steel market. A major element in our program involves obtaining more accurate data on exports and imports of both carbon
steel and specialty steel. This is intended to ensure that Canada is not used as a back door to the U.S. market for offshore suppliers. Monitoring will provide a better appreciation of the complexities of our steel trade, not only with the United States, but with all countries.
As Members know, there are continuing pressures in the United States for Canada to reduce its share of the U.S. steel market. We believe that Canadian steel is fairly traded and that trade restrictive measures at the U.S. or any other border are not warranted. We expect the United States administration to continue resisting pressures from the U.S. industry and Congress to deal fairly with steel imports from Canada.
It is our view that the monitoring program, which will be implemented as a result of the amendment to the Export and Import Permits Act, will be very useful both to the Government and to the industry in resisting American pressures against Canadian imports.
One of the major characteristics of trade in steel between Canada and the United States is its integrated and mutually beneficial nature. We do not restrict access of American steel into our country. In fact, steel imports from the United States average about 5 per cent of the Canadian market and about one-quarter of our total steel imports. For every dollar of steel Canadian primary producers export to the United States, they import about $1.30 worth of equipment and materials from the United States.
Carbon steel has been subject to monitoring under the provisions of the Export and Import Permits Act since September, 1986. This arrangement was introduced on the basis of a recommendation from the Canadian Import Tribunal. It has been successful in producing very useful and timely information on carbon steel imports into Canada. However, with respect to steel exports, there is currently no provision in the Export and Import Permits Act that would let the Government introduce a similar program for exports. This amendment will overcome this problem. Furthermore, to ensure that we have a comprehensive program in place for imports and exports of all steel and reflecting the industry's desire for full coverage, the amendment will enable the Government to monitor imports of specialty steel.
This amendment provides for monitoring for a period of up to three years and is specific to the steel situation. It does not affect other products, nor does it alter the existing criteria under which any other goods may be placed under the import and export controls.
This amendment provides only for the collection of information and both import and export permits will be freely issued. It is not a measure to introduce controls.
The amendment requires us to provide Parliament with an annual statistical summary of information as soon as possible after the end of each calendar year. We believe that this information will generate a better appreciation of the complexities in the steel trade. We will, of course, publish regular
May 27, 1987

monthly reports for the trade. These will normally be issued within a matter of days following the end of each month.
Once the monitoring program is in place and the data on trade flows are available, it will provide a very accurate and precise picture of our trade in steel products with the United States and other countries. This, we believe, will help to ensure that our access to the U.S. market will remain open and that it will dispel any misunderstanding about the nature of Canadian steel exports.
In the period since I announced the monitoring program, we have consulted with all segments of the industry and told them of the general thrust of the monitoring program. We have been assured of the full support of the industry in this initiative. Many industry suggestions will be reflected in the administrative guidelines I will be announcing.
I am well aware of the views of some exporters that controls are inevitable. They may think that it will be to their long-term advantage to raise their level of exports in the immediate future, in the belief that they will eventually gain a higher quota. I do not expect that such controls will become a reality, but let me be very clear that increased exports will not be rewarded, and exporters should be aware of this.
We have continued to work toward maintaining free access to the United States. Consultations have been held between the parliamentary and congressional steel caucuses under the capable leadership of the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling). The parliamentary steel caucus has held several meetings with its U.S. counterpart and, as a result of such meetings, we believe that a better understanding has been reached.
Hear, hear!

The Hon. Member, with good reason, applauds. In addition, Canadian officials have been meeting on a quarterly basis with their U.S. counterparts. Canada and the U.S. steel industry and labour representatives have frequent contact through trade associations, unions and other organizations. These continuing contacts are particularly important in identifying the issues and avoiding conflict, which is in all our interests.
Hon. Members will appreciate that other important initiatives have been taken by the Government in support of our steel policy. For instance, in late August of 1985, country of origin marking requirements were introduced for imported steel pipes and tubes. As I mentioned, an import monitoring system for carbon steel became effective in September, 1986, and in the February, 1987 Budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced the withdrawal of the general preferential tariff on steel imports.
Clearly it is essential for both Government and the private sector to have the best possible data available on steel trade as
Export and Import Permits Act
soon as possible. This amendment will permit the collection of such data and allow us to disseminate it quickly.

Mr. Speaker, as we have previously indicated, it would be the intention of the Official Opposition to support this initiative which was brought forward by the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) and to expedite, as quickly as possible, its passage in this House.
We certainly accept the argument that this particular measure can provide some response to the various pressures which have been put forward by members of the U.S. steel industry and, perhaps more particularly, by certain members of the U.S. Congress who have suggested that Canada has become a staging ground for trans-shipments of steel from countries which are presently subject to the U.S. voluntary restraint program. I think we have been quite insistent all along that that should not be a major factor in affecting the flow of steel between the two countries.
I think the argument has certainly been made clear over time that the increase in the percentage of the steel market occupied by Canadian exports is as much due to the increased demand by U.S. steel manufacturers themselves for Canadian product because of their own labour or market conditions.
I certainly join with the Minister in supporting the work which has been done by Members of Parliament in the steel caucus representing the three Parties. I believe they have undertaken a very important educational program and have been a large contributor to the level of discussion which has taken place.
I would want to use a few moments during my remarks, however, to look at this legislation and raise some questions and perhaps some cautions about what it suggests. First, there have been certain remarks made by the Minister publicly; in fact she made a statement today which does provide a certain slight jar to the hearing. In an interview which was given and reported in The Globe and Mail just after the announcement of the Bill there was a suggestion that this was an evolutionary process.
The question, of course, is what are we evolving toward? Is this seen as a first or another step toward more of a control system being imposed by the United States? When the Minister provided a caution today to Canadian manufacturers, who attempt to inflate their exports into the United States, that that would not be considered, does that mean that something further is on the books? I do not want to draw direct conclusions but I think it would be important for the Minister, perhaps at report stage, as we move through today, to clarify that we are seeing these amendments to the Export Import Act as a terminal step and not necessarily as one of a series of steps which will be taken; that we are simply softening the ground.
I also want to point out that the procedure which has gone on in coming to grips with the dispute and discussion between

May 27, 1987
Export and Import Permits Act
the two countries, does demonstrate the utility and effectiveness of looking at trade between the two countries in a sectoral fashion. One of the interesting and important historical experiences of Canada-U.S. trade has been that we have worked out trade problems on a sectoral basis. Of course, the most obvious example has been the automobile industry where we have a managed trade arrangement which has been certainly beneficial to both sides.
There have been a number of similar cases over the years in which trade disputes have arisen on both sides of the border. By way of different scale and spectrum of trade arrangements, whether by changes in legislation or by rules, understandings or various accords, we have been able to resolve those differences at a reasonably minimal price to the limits of own Parliamentary, political and governmental ways of doing things.
I would suggest to the Minister, who has often admonished Members of this House that the only answer to trade disputes with the United States is a broad comprehensive free trade agreement, that in fact the legislation she is introducing today is another way of doing it. It is an alternative. It does demonstrate that we can resolve these matters, that we can come to grips with these matters on a sectoral basis, on a product by product basis. That has worked in the past and is clearly working in this situation.
I would simply suggest that one of the reasons we find it easier to support this Bill is that it does support one of our own contentions; that is, when it comes to the matter of resolving trade disputes and responding to protectionists measures there are ways of doing it which does not involve the heavy price which would be encountered in a comprehensive, all inclusive, free trade arrangement. When Government spokespersons, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on down, say there is no alternative, 1 suggest to the Minister that we are glad to see that the Government does not always believe its own rhetoric and is prepared to adopt different ways of coming to grips with these measures. I think that is certainly important as we continue the ongoing trade discussions with the United States.
I would suggest that with more diligence and application, similar kinds of results and positive constructions could be put upon other areas where trade disputes also occur. One does not have to resort to the "all or nothing" approach, which is presently the position adopted by the Government opposite.
I would also like to suggest that we hope this is not necessarily the end of the discussion, as far as the Government is concerned, relating to the broader issue of the steel industry in Canada. 1 recognize that the Minister who introduced this legislation is speaking only from a trade aspect and that her colleagues in the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and others who have economic portfolios such as the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin), should be looking at the broader issues of the steel industry. We recognize that there is a big issue out there which is not addressed by this legislation; the production capacity for steel in the world far exceeds the
consumption. The modernization that is taking place in a variety of countries such as Brazil, Taiwan, other Pacific Rim countries, and even some European countries, will continue to place pressure on traditional steel companies.
On the trade side, what that really means is that coming to grips with this issue by way of the GATT negotiations will be very crucial. It also suggests that there has to be some clear understanding, at least by way of industrial guidelines, as to where the steel industry in Canada will be seeking its markets, and to what extent we will be able to continue in our modernization programs, our research and development and in improvement of our technology.
One of the most important features to be emphasized in this whole examination is the reason the Canadian steel industry is running into some static from the Americans. It is that we are better steel producers in key areas. We have modernized our plants and we have improved the technology. That has compared very favourably with the traditional and somewhat obsolete steel plants in the United States.
1 can recall reading the comments of one economic observer back in the late seventies when United States Steel was responding to a number of pressures on the stock market to inflate its stock value so that it would not be taken over and have to go through all the shenanigans of takeover and acquisition. He said it was exceedingly strange that U.S. Steel, which is the largest U.S. producer, was spending hundreds of millions of dollars on the acquisition of Marathon Oil as opposed to putting its money into improving its steel products.
I think that is a lesson that is only now being learned in the U.S. steel industry. Its industry is allowed to use its capital to invest in a number of industries totally incidental to its own product, something which does not improve a product, that does not come to grips with the need to rationalize and to improve the industry which is now suffering that type of competition.
Fortunately, our own steel producers did not respond to that. That is one of the reasons it is important to maintain Canadian ownership of our industries. I think there is a clear record which demonstrates that through Canadian ownership we make much better choices in this key manufacturing sector than many foreign operators have done.
I hope that along the way we will be able to see a more clear-cut steel policy. That does not mean intervention or necessarily that we will be throwing money at the problem. I am not suggesting that. But I do believe that the kind of cooperation that has been evidenced in coming to grips with this specific problem might continue. There could be a broader application of that co-operative sense in the steel industry, certainly with respect to where it fits into the large Canadian picture and where in fact government regulation and efforts must be used.

We must recognize that we do have continuing problems in our own industry. There are major lay-offs taking place at Algoma that must be faced. Workers are being deeply affected by that. So far there has been very little done in the way of adjustment programs to assist those workers.
There is an ongoing problem with Sysco in Cape Breton. It is an industry of major importance to the East Coast and to the Cape Breton region. We understand that there may be a certain countervail applied to it in the United States in terms of steel rails. Where does that fit into the question of procurement?
I again raise the question, under a free trade agreement in which we apply the concept of national treatment to procurement, will the type of privileged position that has been offered up to now to Sysco to sell steel rail to Canadian National and others no longer be acceptable? It could no longer apply under the principles of national treatment. The Minister mentioned in her speech that that would be the guideline that would be applied under a free trade arrangement. We would have to accept a national treatment concept.
I see that my friend from Regina is in the Chamber. He clearly has the interest of IPSCO at heart. Over the years IPSCO has received subsidies, support and preferences from the Government of Saskatchewan and from the federal Government. In terms of the new subsidy legislation that is coming in there cannot be subsidies directed to specific industries. That type of preferential program for parts of the steel industry will no longer be available. Therefore the concept that we have had up until now, that the steel industry is a national steel industry and that it deserves attention on both the East Coast and in western Canada, will be in some jeopardy.
I must say that none of those questions have been answered. We have not received any detailed elaboration in terms of the future of the steel industry, particularly with respect to those parts of it that I have just mentioned. If a signature is put to paper within three, four or five months by the chief trade negotiators on both sides, then clearly the steel industry in Canada will be facing quite substantial and serious questions. I am not referring to those which are in specialized areas, but certainly the ones that I have mentioned, as well as others. They will no longer be able to face that.
I see that the Hon. Member for Burlington, who has been the chairman of the steel caucus, is in the Chamber. 1 know that he and I have shared some differences of opinion about trade over time. I suggest this might be an issue that the steel caucus will want to look at. I think it is a matter of some concern to members of my Party which deal with this matter.
I am not attempting to talk out the clock, Mr. Speaker. It is not often that we get an opportunity to talk about the steel industry in this Chamber. I wish to use this opportunity to raise the type of questions that I have raised and to point out that there are lessons to be learned, that there are issues that we must address.
