Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in the debate on Bill C-57. As has been mentioned by the Minister and by the spokesperson for the Liberal Party, this Bill will receive all-Party support. I think everyone is in favour of it. I know that everyone in the steel industry is in favour of it. Those in management and in labour have been asking for this type of legislation for some time.
As has been explained in the remarks of the Minister and in the remarks of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), the Canadian steel industry is facing some problems, particularly with respect to its exports to the United States. The protectionist mood in the United States, coupled with the serious problems that the American steel industry is facing on the whole, has created ongoing pressures within the United States to restrict the importation of steel, including Canadian steel.
As has been pointed out, the voluntary restraint agreement that the United States has with a series of steel-producing countries restricts the amount of steel that those countries can export into the American market. It has been alleged that some of those countries get around the voluntary restraint agreement by shipping their steel through Canada and having it enter into the American market as Canadian steel. Of course this legislation will, hopefully, if not prevent then at least be able to verify that this is happening and the degree to which it is occurring.
I think it is certainly in the interests of Canadian steel producers, Canadian steelworkers and Members of Parliament from all political Parties, to make certain that the steel that is being exported into the United States is Canadian steel. We are certainly in support of anything that would help prevent steel from VRA countries entering into the United States as Canadian steel.
The Minister was quite right in pointing out that the Canadian relationship with the United States is quite different, especially when it comes to steel. The Minister also pointed out in terms of steel products that for every dollar we export into the American market, the Americans export $1.30 in steel products to Canada.
One could refer to many examples in this area. For example, IPSCO, which is in my district, imports most of its scrap from the United States. Many steel mills in eastern Canada use American coal. Our relationship with the United States in terms of steel is indeed a special one. It is not the same as the

May 27, 1987
Export and Import Permits Act
relationships which Brazil, Japan, and Germany have with the United States. It is a special relationship, and I think it deserves special attention and consideration by the United States.
I would tend to think that the area of adequate information and statistics has been weak on both sides of the border. The American ability to determine how much they actually export into Canada, particularly with the deregulation of the transportation industry, has resulted in some statistics which have not been all that valid. I think the Americans are recognizing this and are boning up their ability to collect data at the border. Certainly the Bill would enable Canada to develop better statistics so we would have a more accurate picture of what we are exporting into the United States.
Let us not be fooled. If some producers wish to circumvent the legislation or the intent of the legislation, they can still do so.
At their peril.

Yes, but there is no clause in the legislation which would punish those producers.
What is also missing in the legislation is the demand that the originating mill be listed. I know that in some circumstances, particularly in this day and age of bartering and swaps, this would be difficult. However, I think it would be helpful to have in the legislation that the application and the permit must show the mill where the steel products originate. As I mentioned, this might be difficult in some circumstances.
I was made aware by the chairman of the steel caucus, the Hon. Member for Burlington, that he spoke with Japanese steel makers who told him of an incident in which they had traded with another country for coffee. The Brazilians were interested in getting its coffee off the market, so they traded steel. The steel was swapped. It had several different owners. By the time it reached its destination, one could not really tell its origin. I recognize that in some circumstances it will be difficult to determine the originating mill.
If we are to have adequate data, we must make an attempt to determine what country produced the steel products we are importing and exporting. Only in that way could we verify what countries or what particular mills are trying to get around their voluntary restraint agreements with the United States. Only in that way would we be able to demonstrate that particular mills and countries are using Canada as a means of laundering their steel.
The world situation in steel is quite bleak. There is tremendous over-production and over capacity for steel and steel products. In years ahead we will see that the world-wide industry will have to be rationalized. We just do not know who will be the winners and the losers. We must make certain that Canadian steel workers and mills are left in the game. When the industry gets itself straightened out and when the dust settles, we must ensure that there is a viable steel industry in Canada.
Of course there is a major problem with the steel industry in the United States. That is not to say that all American steel mills have antiquated and obsolete equipment; there are some quite efficient steel mills, particularly along their West Coast. They are not huge mills. They are smaller and have more up to date equipment. They are technologically more advanced. They produce steel at a very cost efficient price. However, large, traditional steel producers, particularly those in the east, did not think ahead. It was a case of greed. They took all the profits and either used them to acquire other interests or to disburse it to shareholders. What they did not do was reinvest in new plant and equipment.
The result today is that some of the major steel producers in the United States are quite sick and are on the brink of going bankrupt. If some of them go bankrupt, it would be catastrophic, not only to local communities, steel workers, and the pension plans of retired steel workers, but to the economies of the States in which they are located. It would also shake up some of the secondary suppliers, many of whom are Canadian concerns. All of us who are interested in the question of steel share a concern that some of the major players in the United States are on the brink of filing for bankruptcy.
I should like to conclude my remarks by mentioning the steel caucus of which I am a member and of which the Hon. Member for Burlington has been the chairman. The steel caucus is an example of how Parliament and parliamentarians can work. We do not attempt to score political points at the expense of each other. We have a common interest: the viability of the Canadian steel industry in its total sense-not only management or the shareholders, but the steel workers. Our mutual concern allows us to work in a co-operative manner and on behalf of our country and its steel industry. It allows us to lobby on behalf of Canada in the United States and to help engender and bring forth beneficial public policy. It is an example of how Parliament can and should work in many other areas. It is not a matter of ideological differences between political Parties. Members of Parliament work together toward the common good, coming to common sense solutions rather than playing politics at the expense of common sense solutions and the common good. I wish to express to you, Mr. Speaker, that the steel caucus is one example; I think it is an excellent example of how parliamentarians can take a different track and work together toward common sense solutions. As Members of Parliament we can be proud of the steel caucus and the very capable leadership given by the chairman, the Hon. Member for Burlington.
Hear, hear!

I do not wish to take up much more time on Bill C-57. It has the support of our caucus and Members. We are concerned with one or two things that we would like to address when the Bill gets to Committee of the Whole.
May 27, 1987

Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions among the Parties and I think you will find unanimous consent for this Bill to be sent to Committee of the Whole House rather than a legislative committee. I understand there is a willingness to dispose of all three stages of the Bill this afternoon. I would also advise the House that the Minister during clause by clause study will have officials in the House to answer any questions which Members of the Opposition may have.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly have no objection to the statement made by the Parliamentary Secretary, but I want to ensure that what he has proposed takes place after second reading has concluded. I think there are still some people in the House who would like to continue with second reading.
Obviously, yes, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to indicate on behalf of the New Democratic Party that we concur with this arrangement. We will be pleased to see this Bill pass all stages today.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to thank the Official Opposition, particularly the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), and the Member from the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong), for their co-operation in the passage of this Bill. The Member from Regina East made reference to the steel caucus that I happen to be fortunate enough to chair, and I might say that the caucus is made up of a fine group of people. Indeed, we are non-political. We work on behalf of the steel industry and I applaud them for their assistance and good counsel when difficult issues arise.
This legislation before us today was requested firstly by the steel industry and secondly by the steelworkers of Canada. The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) and her officials had long and serious discussions with the various elements of the steel trade in Canada, not only with the industry and the United Steelworkers of America, but also with those in the steel service centres, in secondary production and those in the steel fabricating end of the industry. All agreed that this legislation should come forward. We have tried to deal with how to get a handle on the monitoring of steel exported from Canada for some time, but with little or no success and so we have moved to this monitoring stage.
1 would like to review briefly why we had to come to this stage. The American industry has experienced some difficulties. In 1984, the U.S. Department of Commerce became aware that about 26 per cent of the American steel market was dominated by imported steel. An effort was made to put quotas and restrictions on the importers and the exporters of steel in the American market. Much of that steel was being dumped onto the American market. Canada was exempted from a voluntary restraint agreement quota at that time. We were not and have not, to the best of my knowledge, ever dumped steel on the American market. Odd cases have gone before the International Trade Commission, and there have
Export and Import Permits Act
been anti-dumping investigations here and there, but by and large the process that we have in place, and that the Americans have in place, has taken care of any distortions that may have appeared on the price side of the steel business.
Initially the steel manufacturers complained that the price of steel was being unfairly depressed in the American marketplace because imported steel was coming in at low and dumped prices. The administration moved to what it called the VRA, the voluntary restraint agreement, which was signed with about 19 countries. For a portion of the apparent American market they were not to countervail or anti-dump and were to abide by the voluntary restraint agreement. Canada, not being a part of that arrangement, did not have a commitment. Our traditional share of the American market at that time was about 3 per cent. Our primary producers being very responsible people said they would endeavour to maintain our share of the American market at about 3 per cent. They have done that fairly well until recently.
In any commercial arrangement, people after a while find avenues of escape. What we have found, and the Americans have concurred with us, is that there have been some purchasers of steel in the U.S., other than producers, who have been buying steel from countries which have signed a VRA with the Americans. When the steel quota assigned to a particular country runs out they have shipped steel into a facility here in Canada, into a warehouse, a bonding house or something of that nature. Then the steel is trans-shipped into the United States and is counted as Canadian steel, which is clearly unfair to our producers. Our difficulty is that we do not know the dimension, the dynamics, the size, the amount involved, but we know that happens.
My colleague from Regina East has also made mention of steel found in counter-trade. Counter-trade is a practice that is becoming more and more important in the world. Some Third World countries which have put steel exporting facilities and steel production facilities together have found that they could trade semi-finished steel, billets or raw steel to other countries in exchange for other commodities required. That steel is floating around in warehouses in the Third World waiting for a place to park. Some of it could find its way into Canada. If so, it would be transformed in some way and would enter the American market and counted as Canadian steel. Therefore, we had to move to see how we could get a handle on how much was involved and if we could ensure that it was not counted as Canadian steel.
We had discussions in Washington last week with officials of the American Iron and Steel Institute and with the executives of the congressional steel caucus on the monitoring Bill. I can say that we were well received. Officials from the Departments of International Trade and External Affairs did an outstanding job in presenting the monitoring Bill and the regulations behind it to the officials.

May 27, 1987
Export and Import Permits Act
I must say that the Americans were very impressed with the speed with which we were able to move with legislation as compared to the speed of their process, bearing in mind that the United States is a larger country with more people and more complex issues. They were openly complimentary about the way we could talk about a problem and then, in a very short period of time, put together a program and tell them what it was.
The Americans feel that what we are doing will be effective. For the first time, it will provide clear information about the origin of steel entering the American market. I think that will help our companies tremendously.
The other point we tried to make is that our mill-to-mill shipments should be exempt from any agreed to or voluntary quota in the American market. In fact, when we ship steel from our mills to their mills, we are helping their steel industry. As Hon. Members are aware, there have been shutdowns, strikes and bankruptcies in the American steel industry and when we make mill-to-mill shipments, we act almost like a just-in-time supplier.
Many people know what steel is, but they do not know the politics of steel. It is a very political business. Canada is the largest customer of the United States steel industry. As the Minister pointed out, we buy about 500,000 tonnes, worth something in the neighbourhood of $450 million per year to the Americans. As well, the United States is our largest customer. It is a relationship that is unparalleled. There are no two other countries in the world trading in a commodity like steel with the relationship we have with the United States of America.
Canada buys 90 per cent of its metallurgical coal from Tennessee, Virginia and Pennsylvania. As well, about 45 per cent of the pellets used in Canada are bought from American mines. In fact, we own some of the coal and iron ore mines. The Canadian steel industry owns several steel facilities in the United States, facilities which employ about 12,000 Americans. Truly we have a relationship that is unparalleled and unequalled in the world.
When we go there, one of our great difficulties in the hustle and bustle of Washington is getting our colleagues to recognize our relationship. We tell them we are not Brazil, Taiwan or Korea, we are Canada. We spend $1.30 in the American market for every dollar we ship in and we are the United States' largest customer. We trade facilities back and forth. We send steel to the United States for a process that is not done in Canada and indeed we receive American steel for heat treating because there is no comparable facility in the United States. Our arrangement is very unique, and our objective in this legislation is to see that that relationship continues and is not diminished in any way.
What happens in most commercial relationships is that a VRA is put on in an attempt to have a measure of control over a situation, but then people find a way to circumvent the VRA.
That has happened here and that is what we are trying to correct. We want to know the country of origin of steel going into the United States. For all we know, some of the American steel that comes into Canada and is processed here and then returned to the United States may be going into the United States as Canadian steel. We do not know that but we will find out through this monitoring process.
In the years since 1984, when the VRA system was put in place by the American Government, the number of companies shipping steel into the United States has increased. I was absolutely flabbergasted when I learned that there are approximately 700 companies shipping steel into the United States. There are 14 primary producers in Canada but there are 700 companies shipping steel into the United States. Of those companies, 350 have emerged in the last couple of years.
We must realize that there are a great many people involved in this trade and we simply do not know the depth of it. We do not know if some of these companies are operating out of a telephone booth, out of a steel warehouse or out of a mill that transforms steel. We simply do not know the dimensions of it and the monitoring Bill will allow the Minister for International Trade to monitor the situation. When my colleagues in the steel caucus and our officials go to the United States to talk to the American administration and the Congressional authorities, we will be able to do so armed with some good, hard information that will help us make our case.
We have much to gain by putting this legislation in place. When it was originally brought forward by the Minister, her officials, her Parliamentary Secretary and others sat down with opposition Members and told them the story. Opposition Members listened to what we wanted to do and they agreed. I think that is a fine example of how Parliament can work when serious matters that have to be dealt with in an expeditious way come before it.
I look forward to hearing other comments. I understand the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) will make some comments on this matter and I look forward to hearing what she has to say. Then I look forward to going through the other stages of this Bill and to its final passage. I am told that the Senate will handle it in the same fashion. This is a good example of how we can do things when they have to be done.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, a number of Hon. Members have outlined the situation facing the Canadian steel industry and have indicated why this Bill is before us today. We in the Opposition will support the Bill. If the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) were present, he would certainly have said that he himself has been asking for this legislation in the form of questions in the House. We are pleased to see that the Government has taken the initiative which was launched by Canadian steel producers as well as the labour movement.
May 27, 1987

Indeed, this is a very good example of how dealing with trade on a sectoral basis is working. The steel industry is a good example of how Canada and the United States have historically been able to hammer out solutions to cross-border problems that vex both countries.
One thing we have not touched on is the reason for the malaise in the American steel industry. While I know U.S. Senator Heinz is motivated to bring forth protectionist legislation merely to ward off competition from a number of countries, Canada among them, one reason is that the plants in the U.S. have not been modernized. They have not received the support from Government that we have. I might say that past Liberal Governments have been in a position to permit modernization of the steel industry so that Dofasco and Stelco, the two major steel companies in Canada, both in my riding, have among the most modern plants in the world. The companies, in concert with workers and Government, moved very early on to modernize their facilities.
A second issue relates to the fact we in Canada have had the export edge. This is because of the inflated value of the American dollar. Unfortunately, some of the measures being considered in the U.S. Congress to deal with the so-called steel import problem are really tied to that fact. That in turn, because of our close proximity as well as our first-class product, has given us an edge in the American market.
The Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) pointed out that we have 14 major steel producers in Canada. The major players have worked very closely to try to develop a good working relationship with the U.S. so that we would not be forced to accept a voluntary restraint agreement. We know that people like Don Belch and Bob Varah of Stelco and Dofasco have been working together, going to Washington on a regular basis. Any time I phone Stelco it usually turns out that Mr. Belch is working in Washington to try to convince the Americans of what we in Canada already know, that is, that we are fair trading partners, we are not dumping steel. In the isolated cases of alleged steel dumping which have been brought to the attention of the Americans, we have actually seen a situation where some of these maverick companies, those which are jobbing steel from third countries via Canada into the U.S. because the importing of steel from those countries is limited, have set up subsidiary companies in Canada which they use to divert steel from third countries through Canada into the U.S. We have seen that in the case of a couple of concrete floor manufacturers in the U.S. who import steel rod from other countries via Canada. In fact, the American entrepreneur is subverting his own legislation and the Canadian steel industry is taking the brunt of criticism for the alleged increase in the amount of steel imports into the U.S.
I think the other issue that was lightly touched on by the Hon. Member for Burlington is the fact that for every dollar we sell to the U.S. we consume $1.30 in imported product to
Export and Import Permits Act
make steel. We should emphasize that point. When the U.S. Congress is dealing with the increase in steel imports they also must realize they are benefiting directly through the sale of goods to Canada to the tune of $1.30 for every dollar we sell to the U.S.
I know that a number of editorialists and a number of Americans have pointed to what I would characterize as a small blip in the U.S. import market in the early part of this year. The reason for that blip has been articulated by other Members, but when USX went on strike I spoke to steel producers in Hamilton who told me they were being begged to sell our first quality steel to the U.S. Of course they chose not to fill the orders because they did not want to create a situation where Canadian imports increased so much as to encourage any further protectionist action by the U.S.
Notwithstanding the fact that the Canadian steel industry, through the Canadian Steel Producers Association as well as the steelworkers and their tripartite approach with the Government, has literally bent over backwards to inhibit any thinking in the U.S. Congress that Canada is not a fair trading partner, we continue to be assaulted by claims of dumping. One of the elements of discussion raised in the House over the last number of months has been the allegation of dumping of Canadian steel being considered by the U.S. Department of Commerce.
When you look at the telex which deals with the allegations you see they are being levelled at companies which are not even producing the particular type of steel about which the allegations are made. In fact, there has been absolutely no substance at all to American claims about dumping by Stelco and Algoma Steel, for example. These companies are prepared to go to the U.S. Department of Commerce and fight their case. They will win. We have done it in the past and we will continue to do it. Yet at the same time we are tying up valuable dollars and the valuable time of some of our top people who go back and forth to the U.S. constantly lobbying on issues which have been won time and time again. If we adopted a sectoral approach to making sure that Canadian steel producers are able to sell our top quality products in the U.S. without being aggravated at every turn by congressional protectionist measures, it would receive the support of all Canadians.
I remember that a couple of years ago, when the Government was in the process of launching its free trade initiative, a secret document was leaked to the press. It dealt with what kind of strategies the Opposition should be approached with. That document suggested that Members who represented steel-producing ridings, like myself, were particularly vulnerable and must de facto support a trade agreement because in effect the steel industry would be a potential beneficiary. Our response is that time and time again we have shown, through our producers and our labour movement, that we are prepared to deal with the questions of U.S. protectionism as they are raised on an ongoing basis.

May 27, 1987
Export and Import Permits Act
I think this legislation is another attempt by Parliament, with the assistance and support of the trade unions as well as the management of most of our steel companies, to deal with the problem and head it off at the pass. It will work to show the Americans we are very serious about maintaining the quota of exports to the U.S. at around the 3.5 per cent or 3.7 per cent level. I think 3.7 per cent is the level which certainly Mr. Varah has publicly stated we were prepared to live with. As long as we show this good faith in Parliament as well as in the steel industry we should be in a position to convince the Americans that we mean fair business but we intend to protect our share of the steel market.
My concern in the long term is that the American Government will see weakness in the Canadian position. It will see weakness in our position as it did when the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) went to Washington on the softwood lumber deal. The Minister said, "We are prepared to saw off and make you an offer, and if that offer does not work, it is our final offer". Yet she subsequently came back with a second final offer and so on.
If the American Congress perceives a weakness in the position of the Canadian Government, if it sees blood, it is going to go for the jugular. If it goes for the jugular and is successful in introducing protectionist measures as they affect the Canadian steel industry, we run the risk of losing tens of thousands of Canadian jobs.
1 certainly support the measure that is being introduced today by the Government. I think it is long overdue and I think it will send a signal to the United States that the Canadian steel industry is very serious about being a fair trading partner and that we are prepared to put our reputation on the line, prepared to say that we do not want steel to be diverted from third countries through Canada merely to subvert the voluntary restraint agreement, that by God we do not want any more possibility for export control curbs from Canada to the United States and we do not want a VRA imposed on Canada.
We have heard the President say that Canada's steel industry will continue to be able to trade with the United States, but we have also seen him circle the wagons when need be. In introducing this legislation in Parliament and in getting the support of the steel producers and the labour movement, the Minister for International Trade must send that message to Washington in the strongest possible terms. If we can do it through the steel caucus or through debate here in the Houses of Parliament, that is terrific.
However, it must be done. We have to tell Washington that these export control curbs are being put in place so that we can prove once and for all that we are fair trading partners and are not dumping our steel into the United States.
We can pass this legislation with a clean conscience, but we must ensure that the Americans, including Senator Heinz, get the message loud and clear. Far too much Canadian time and
energy is currently being spent fighting phantom legal battles in Washington following allegations of dumping such as those recently put before the Department of Commerce. Enough Canadian steel producers have shown that we are prepared to play ball. We have to protect our option because as the American dollar reaches a more reasonable level the world strata of steel sales could change. It is important that we recognize that.

Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say it is a good thing that the support for this Bill is unanimous, because it gives the Canadian Government a strong position from which to tell Americans that we have already gone far enough to prove we are fair and equitable producers, that we are not about to sell steel from other countries across Canada, to try and circumvent U.S. regulations. Our conscience is pretty clear on that, and we would like to pass this Bill to convince Americans they should not react by passing a lot of new protectionist legislation in the U.S.
Mr. Speaker, I think that with this Bill, with the unanimous support of producers and workers, opposition Parties and the Government, we can send a fairly strong message to the Minister for International Trade. We can give him the strength to tell the Americans we do not want to be subject to so-called voluntary restrictions. I think we should not give Americans the impression that we are weak-kneed on this point, which was the case in the softwood lumber affair, where we had a weak Minister, a Minister who promised, who made a final offer and who in the final instance made a second and a third final offer. We do not want the same thing to happen in the steel industry because thousands of jobs would be lost if the Americans decided to impose a restrictive, so-called voluntary agreement, which is a contradiction in terms since restrictions are never voluntary. We are prepared to support the Government, but we want it to speak with a strong voice. We are concerned, and not just about this Bill, but generally speaking, that the policy set forth by the Government so far in our free trade talks gives the Americans the impression that we are not speaking from strength but from weakness. We must speak with a strong voice to protect jobs in the steel industry and in other sectors. And that is why we in the Liberal Party are prepared to support this Bill.

I would like to conclude by asking the Minister to consider the possibility of introducing further legislation containing a real steel policy. In essence, this is fire-fighting at an early stage, but it is not dealing with the situation at Sysco and in other regions of the country where the steel industry is essentially being deindustrialized. We are lucky in the City of Hamilton that in the first fiscal quarter of 1987 The Steel Company of Canada showed a profit. Dofasco did not show a profit for the reason that it is writing off some of its modernization improvements, but it had a pre-tax profit. We are doing very well in Hamilton and are fair trading partners.
May 27, 1987
Thanks to a good Government.

The Minister says "thanks to a good Government". It is actually thanks to a great workforce in the City of Hamilton. Our workers, both at The Steel Company of Canada and at Dofasco, are producing the best quality product in the world thanks to previous Liberal Governments which permitted them to have the most state of the art equipment available. They have a one-track rolling process which allows our steel to be as competitive as any found in any country, even when pitted against the low salaries paid in Korea, Brazil, and some other countries.
We are the number one steel-producing community in the world. Hamilton East is the number one steel riding in Canada. That is because past Liberal Governments had the foresight to recognize that we had to modernize and upgrade the industry and not allow the type of deterioration of plants that we have seen in the United States. That is why Pittsburgh is in the mess in which it is at the moment. American Governments did not have the same foresight as the Canadian Government. In addition, we have the best workforce in the world, so it is natural that we should be doing well.
However, there are other parts of the country which are not doing that well. I think about Sydney, Regina, and other areas of the country which need help. I do not think this particular measure goes far enough toward actually introducing a steel policy which will deal with the deindustrialization which is occurring in some of the less fortunate areas of the country in the steel industry.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join my colleague, other members of the Official Opposition, and Members on the government side in speaking in support of this legislation which is quite clearly not intended to establish a steel policy however needful we might be of the development of such a policy. We have before us a piece of legislation which will complete the cycle of the monitoring system initiated as a result of last year's report of the Canadian Import Tribunal with regard to carbon steel which established the requirement for import permits. This legislation would impose a requirement for export permits.
There has been a great deal said about the state of the steel industry world-wide and the conditions which have evolved over the last little while. This topic was dealt with in quite considerable detail in the report of the Canadian Import Tribunal which points out that changes in the kinds of material used in manufacture, the entry of Third World countries into the field of steel production, the development of an overcapacity matched by the use of subsidies and import controls in many nations historically involved in the export of steel have created a situation which has posed, poses, and will pose a danger to our steel industry and the steel industry of the United States.
Export and Import Permits Act
It has been indicated that the reaction of Senator Heinz to the state of affairs in Pennsylvania is not very different from the kind of reaction expressed by those who speak on behalf of those who depend upon the steel industry of Sydney, for example. The threatened imposition of a 2.4 per cent quota on Canadian steel imported into the United States raises the question about the level playing field and the issues of the relative rate of importation of steel into our respective countries. This flies in the face of the agreement reached previously with 18 countries importing steel to the United States to restrain their imports to the United States voluntarily. Canada was omitted from that requirement because it was found not to be engaging in unfair trading practices with respect to steel.
While Canada has restrained itself during this, in an attempt to maintain its 3 per cent traditional level of steel import, we nevertheless face a challenge with respect to steel as we have faced with respect to other items.
It has been noted that the American steel industry has not kept pace with the need for technological change and greater efficiency. The Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) ascribed the failure of the American steel industry to the absence of federal aid to the industry in that country. However, I believe the record will show that many of the large corporations in the United States greedily distributed the profits to shareholders rather than reinvesting in the modernization of the steel industry. Therefore, the fault cannot be exclusively laid at the door of the Government, but must partly be attributed to those who own and operate steel companies.
While the Liberal Government in the past provided some help to the steel industry in Canada, I believe it is evident that the Canadian steel industry had more foresight and therefore did not require the same level of subsidy as other countries in order to modernize and maintain a level of competitiveness. That has allowed it even to exceed the quotas that have been imposed by general agreement because those in the United States who purchase steel recognize the quality of steel that is produced here.
A voluntary restraint agreement was reached with a number of nations that previously not only imported steel but potentially exceeded the levels of importation in the United States. It now seems clear that with Canada's situation becoming somewhat different, they were possibly trying to take advantage of Canada's unique position by trans-shipping cheap steel to the United States after transforming and processing it to a substantial extent to allow such steel to gain access to the United States.
It is important to adopt this legislation so that there is a clear understanding and clear information about the transshipment of steel or the exceeding of the traditional levels of importation of steel in the United States from Canada. It will provide for discussion and agreement with the United States on the basis of sound information. This is very appropriate

May 27, 1987
Export and Import Permits Act
legislation and I hope it will demonstrate that Canada has honestly pursued its voluntary restraints.
While the major exporters of steel have respected restraint, there is some evidence that smaller corporations-some of which may be subsidiaries of American companies-have abused the understanding and taken advantage of a situation that is at least partly created by the Americans who come here and try to sneak steel in from those smaller producers. This legislation will enable us to ascertain whether that is true. We will be able to determine whether the suspicions of people like Senator Heinz are supported by that data. This legislation will give us a basis to argue strongly on Canada's behalf that the same situation not be created with steel as was created with respect to softwood lumber.
The imposition of the import permit in September, 1986, caused considerable concern about steel importation by those associated with the automobile industry where "on-time" delivery and the efficient and rapid transfer of products across the border is very important. I want to congratulate the Government for having found ways to facilitate that rapid processing of permits in order to allay the fears that most manufacturers had about the effect of the permits in terms of automobile production.
Since steel products in the automobile industry go both ways and "on-time" delivery is still as important, I hope the Government will be as forthcoming as it was then in ensuring that the imposition of an export permit requirement will not constitute an impediment to commerce in the export and import of steel in the automobile industry.
On behalf of my Party I am pleased to join with my colleague in support of this legislation and seek its rapid passage and implementation.

speechtext:
Order. House in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-57, an Act to amend the Export and Import Permits Act.
Shall Clause 1 carry?
On Clause 1-Addition to Export Control List or Import Control List

With respect to Clause 1, I want to refer the Minister to a very central question. We know that the purpose of the legislation, particularly in this clause, is to determine whether there is trans-shipment taking place and to ensure that countries are not avoiding or evading the VRA imposed by the United States Government. One of the key questions is how much reprocessing must take place in a Canadian mill using certain foreign steel components before it is considered to be Canadian. Under this clause we have the right to put it on the prohibited list. I suppose the key question is, if we are going to be applying certificates, can the Minister tell us how we are going to determine whether or not it is in fact covered by this particular section?

Mr. Chairman, I could tell the House that the Government is not attempting in this Bill to establish criteria for a substantial transformation or rules of origin on steel. We believe the existing procedures, including auditing, will enable us to identify non-Canadian steel exported to the U.S. We are confident that through close co-operation between the Canadian and U.S. customs authorities, appropriate steps will be taken to ensure that Canada is not used as a back door for foreign steel into the U.S. market.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not sure the Minister quite answered my question. I think we are dealing in an area where perhaps she is prepared to elaborate. I understand Senator John Heinz, who was visiting here in Ottawa, is currently threatening to introduce a new Steel Bill in the United States Senate which would be incorporated in its new Trade Bill, He indicated that one of the problems they face is that Canadian steel for export is in fact a reprocessed steel, transformed from other products. I suppose the question is, if there is nothing in this Bill which captures that, then what will be the response from the United States and our response to that particular issue which has been raised by the United States Senators in discussing their own Trade Bill?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think the Hon. Member is sufficiently aware of the fact that it is up to the Americans to ensure that American law is being kept in this case. We do not intend to run around the border being the policemen for American law. We will co-operate. We will collect statistics. We will transmit those statistics. However, the issue the Hon. Member raises deals with the requirements set by the Americans in their market. I am sure that, given his stand on sovereignty issues in the past, the Hon. Member would not expect us to be the policemen in enforcing American law.

Well, Mr. Chairman, the Minister is certainly right that I would not want the Canadian Government to be involved in setting those standards. One reason I am asking the question is to determine under this section, where the Minister has the right to place certain products on the prohibited list, what those products will in fact incorporate
May 27, 1987

and whether they will take into account that there are various ranges of reprocessing which takes place between using certain steel products and the level of transformation which can be from 5 per cent to 50 per cent, 60 per cent or 70 per cent. I am asking whether we are intending to apply any test of that kind to determine whether or not they would be put on the list. That is the question I am asking.

I have answered that by saying that after looking at this issue and studying it, and seeing whether it would be appropriate, we have decided it is not useful to establish criteria for substantial transformation or the rules of origin issue.
The purpose of this is to monitor steel, and we will be auditing the process so that those companies which in any way indicate they are cheating on the process or incorrectly identifying the origins of steel will be identified.

If I could just follow through on that answer, Mr. Chairman, I think the industry itself has expressed its concern to the Government that if the monitoring process itself is not strong enough, it is wondering if the Government is prepared for further action.
In some ways it is perhaps a hypothetical question at this stage. I am sure the Minister will say: "Well, we are taking this step and then we will see what happens", but I am asking the Minister in essence to put on the record what her thinking is. At what stage would the Government consider taking some other measures?

Mr. Chairman, I hope the Hon. Member is not suggesting that he is pushing or pressing for other measures. Other measures, of course, would get us into controls and voluntary restraints, and this House has worked hard to ensure that this measure is workable and will be productive. Beyond that I think we are very much into a hypothetical question. I am not going to say: "When this process fails, I will consider other things or other steps". I am saying that this process will work, that it will meet the needs for which it was designed.

1 have another concern. Does the Government feel it has the power in Clause 1 to be able to get the data it is seeking? Does the Minister believe she will get in all cases the mill of origin and the country of origin for steel imports and exports?

Mr. Chairman, the answer to the Hon. Member's question is, of course, yes. We have had a lot of consultation with the industry and with the union. We are advised that we will get the information we require in this process because it has been worked out with a lot of consultation from the affected parties. The other measure, which I mentioned earlier in answer to the question from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), is that we are going to be auditing. We are going to have people in the field examining how this system is working. They will be reporting back to us on a continual basis.
Export and Import Permits Act

Will the Minister also have a program in place that the Government will be able to follow with respect to, let us say, steel coming into the country being either reprocessed, altered or not altered at all, so that the Government will be able to follow it through and see how it comes into the country, what happens to it and when and how it gets exported?

Mr. Chairman, I believe I have already answered that by saying that this is the kind of information we are seeking. This process has been designed in consultation with the industry and the union. We are advised that we will get this information as we require it. The auditing process, I think, is a good back-up to ensure we do. If we find that there is some technical way by which we can improve it, of course, we will.

Can the Minister elaborate on the auditing process that will be introduced? Will it take the form of inspection or will it be just a paper examination? What kind of inspection or enforcement system will be put in place?
The audit about which we have talked here will be carried out by the auditing services of the Department of Supply and Services. It will conform to the normal practices of the Department.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to change the focus slightly and ask the Minister if she can tell the House whether this information-gathering system is satisfactory to her counterparts in the United States with whom she has discussed it. Can we assume that the implementation of an information-gathering system, as the Minister has described it, will meet the objections of the Steel Institute, the Commerce Department and the steel Senators?
The reason I raise this question is for a very specific reason. As the Minister knows the Senator from Pennsylvania has suggested that he will be introducing in the Senate the inclusion of a specific trade Bill directed at Canada which would be incorporated into the large omnibus trade Bill which is now on the floor of the Senate. Can the Minister report whether in fact the implementation of this particular measure will succeed, in her estimation, in satisfying those various critics and forestalling those initiatives?

Mr. Chairman, we have had many discussions on this issue with the U.S. Cabinet Ministers involved. It has been raised by my American counterparts on numerous occasions, including just recently at the OECD. They have indicated to me that they are pleased that we have responded to this bilateral irritant in a positive way. Of course, we are happy that we have done this in a made-in-Canada way since a global problem is involved.
At the administration level in the U.S., they are quite prepared to see if this brings forward the type of information for which we are looking. There have been many discussions

May 27, 1987
Export and Import Permits Act
between officials, and the same type of positive response has been forthcoming.
The Hon. Member for Burlington recently returned from talks with the steel caucus. He has advised me that there is great interest in seeing if this can work.
The information that we will be collecting has not been collected before. We are looking to the fact that that information will give us some idea of what the trends are and what is happening both on the import and the export side.
If the Hon. Member is asking whether this will resolve once and for all our problems in the steel trade with the United States, I can say that this is not likely, but it is a good positive step. Everyone is interested in seeing it work. Because of the co-operation that we have had from members of the Opposition on this issue I assume that the Hon. Member is similarly disposed.

Mr. Chairman, on the latter point raised by the Hon. Minister, hopefully the Americans will accept our statistics. Once these amendments have been put through, we will have a much better source of statistics than will the Americans. We will also have better statistics with respect to American imports than what the Americans have concerning their exports of steel to Canada. Hopefully, the Americans will accept our statistics.
1 have one other question which deals with Subclause (3) of Clause 1 which requires the Minister to table the statistical summaries in Parliament as soon as possible at the end of each calendar year. Can the Minister tell us whether or not the Government might be in a position to issue statistics on a more regular basis? The nature of the steel trade right now is that each month's figures are now looked at, and that can affect and influence what is happening in Congress. We often hear that Congressmen are reacting to figures that they received a month prior or the month prior to that. It would certainly be useful if we could have more regular statistics.

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member is a member of the parliamentary steel caucus. He is well aware of the fact that the present steel statistics that are published by the Americans are very often out of whack, to use a colloquial expression. One of the difficulties we face is that by the time the corrected figures are announced, figures which are usually lower than the initial ones, there is a public perception that we are flooding the American market with Canadian steel exports. So everyone in this House and anyone who has been party to this matter would agree that we have had a statistical problem. That is one of the reasons we are suggesting this amendment. It is so that we can collect statistics which will be better. Yes, they will be better than the ones produced by the Americans. That is why we will be transmitting them to and sharing them with the Americans. That is also why we will be publishing them on a monthly basis for the trade, which addresses the Hon. Member's point about when they would be available.
I want to underline that while there will be a monthly publication as soon as possible, there will only be one annual report to Parliament. I think that is perhaps where the Hon. Member may have been confused.
I also want to say that we have suggested to the Americans the setting up of a steel commission which would tackle such problems as the co-ordination of statistics and possibly look in a global fashion at the steel market from a North American perspective. The Americans have expressed interest in such a proposal. However, they have some concerns that it might violate their anti-trust laws. They are presently looking at it and will get back to us on it. That would deal with the problem identified by the Hon. Member.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall Clause 1 carry?
Agreed.

Clause agreed to.
On Clause 2-Import and Export Permits

Mr. Chairman, as I understand Clause 2 it is that the Minister shall issue, upon application, the permits. I have just one concern in this respect. It is to do with the speed with which these permits will be issued. Will there be any problem at all? When an application is made, what sort of timeframe are we looking at in terms of the issuance of the permit?

Mr. Chairman, as I said in my speech, this is not a control program. We would strongly oppose any suggestion that it is a control program. Export and import permits will be freely available on request.
My officials advise me that they will be available from 44 or 48 computerized terminals across the country. So they will be available on an automatic computerized system. I think it will be done as expeditiously as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I take from the Minister's answer that it would be almost automatic. The application is made, the paperwork is put through, and in a matter of days, at most, the permit would be issued, if not sooner.
Under what circumstance would the Minister deny a permit? If a company seeking a permit has a record of falsifying data and for some reason does not want to disclose fully the information requested, would the Minister deny a permit under such circumstances?

Mr. Chairman, in order to respond further to the Hon. Member's question, these terminals are in customs brokers' offices or External Affairs offices, but they are readily available to the trade. We have taken great care to ensure that the terminals and access to the system are where people need them to be.
In terms of refusing permits, a permit would be refused if the information was falsified. I think the system is set up so
May 27, 1987

that if the data is incomplete it is rejected. However, I am not familiar with the squeaks and bugs in the computer system. I would be glad to get more information on the technical operation of the computer system to the Hon. Member if he would desire.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may obtain some clarification from the Minister on the statement she made and on what apparently she has indicated on other occasions in the House that the provisions of Bill C-57, particularly Clause 2, are not intended to be control measures but are designed for the purpose of information gathering.
1 want to indicate to the Minister the nature of my concern. This very day in media reports in the City of Halifax, there was an indication that the proposal to assist Sydney Steel Corporation might result in adverse consequences in that it would be suggested or the allegation would be made, in relation to international trade, particularly with the United States of America, that the Sydney Steel Corporation was being improperly subsidized, and that in turn this would result in or create difficulties in the United States in respect of the fair aspects of trading.
Because the new provisions require the issuance of an export permit in circumstances, I would like to ask the Minister whether there would be any intention at present or in the future that Sydney Steel would be placed in any jeopardy in relation to its trading with the United States because of any assistance it might receive.
On the face of it, the consideration may go beyond the provisions now before the House, but the fact of the matter is that the claim has been made that Sydney Steel, notwithstanding the minute amount of trading it does in steel transactions with the United States, might be creating difficulties in relation to free trade generally and steel trading particularly.
May I point out to the Minister, although I am sure she is aware, that the amount of trading Sydney Steel does with the United States is infinitesimal. In terms of general trading, I think it amounts to less than half of 1 per cent of the amount of steel exported to the United States. Yet it is claimed by some people, particularly other interested parties in the Province of Ontario-and it has even been suggested that it might be coming from Algoma Steel-that any assistance to Sydney Steel could result in serious consequences in terms of our international trade relations in general and steel trading in particular.
If the Minister could clarify that matter in relation to this Bill, I would be indebted to her.

Mr. Chairman, the matters which the Hon. Member raised go far beyond Bill C-57. I do not feel this is the appropriate forum to comment on them.
This legislation has no relation to the issue he raises. The only comment I could make is that the American industry has available to it American trade remedy law. If they feel that there are unfair trade practices, they have recourse under
Export and Import Permits Act
American law. Presumably the tests of that would be not only subsidy but injury.
However, the steel Bill about which we are talking here is to protect our status as a fair trader in steel. It does not deal with the issues the Hon. Member has raised.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 3 agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakeroldname: Miss Carney (for the Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-57, an Act to amend the Export and Import Permits Act, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-57, an Act to amend the Export and Import Permits Act, provides a great deal of assistance to the steel industry. Since 1984, when the United States decided that it would cut back on imports of steel from offshore, the industry has been in tremendous turmoil and great uncertainty.
The problem before us now in steel, with the mentality and attitude of the United States Congress, is the kind of problem with which we will be dealing in the future. The United States Congress, if not the administration, is clearly moving toward an approach of managed trade. I do not believe that that is necessarily the view of the administration of the United States, but it is clearly the view of Congress. Since last November, when the Democrats took charge of the Congress, they have been in the driver's seat and have shown on two recent Bills relating to the water Act and the highways Act that they are clearly in charge in the United States Government.
The Bill really results from the exercise to establish voluntary restraint agreements in 1984. The U.S. administration and the Congress wished to back out from millions and millions of tonnes of steel coming into the U.S. market and from established voluntary restraint agreements with a couple of dozen countries. Some countries were trying to get several million tonnes of steel into the United States. The most obvious access to that tremendous U.S. market was Canada. We have always been fair traders with the United States. Algoma in Sault Ste. Marie buys all of its coal from the U.S. Much of the iron ore, a great deal of supplies and equipment are bought in the United States. The industry is very integrated. The steel caucus of the House of Commons has done a great deal to build an understanding and a liaison with Congressmen in the U.S., who have been going through a terrible time facing the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs in the steel industry. Clearly, when those voluntary restraint agreements were put in place in 1984 and early 1985, our share of the market was something around 3 per cent. In the

May 27, 1987
Export and Import Permits Act
first quarter of 1987, our share jumped dramatically. The pressure was on to prevent that.
There are Bills in the Congress. One is Senator Heinz' Bill which will limit Canada, Taiwan and other countries not under the voluntary restraint agreement to their share of the U.S. market. Hopefully, the legislation before us today to monitor exports to the United States will not only identify which steel is coming from fabricators and processors and which is coming from the basic steel producers, such as Algoma, Dofasco and Stelco, but it will also identify steel coming from Japan, South Korea and Brazil being fabricated, even to a modest extent in Canada, and then being trans-shipped to the United States.
If we find that large volumes of steel are from countries under voluntary restraint agreements with the United States, steel being trans-shipped through Canada will be identified and it will be included in their quotas going into the U.S. As a result, we will be able to secure and stabilize jobs for the basic steel producers, which is extremely important. We are hoping that the oil and gas industry will pick up. Companies like Algoma Steel have had a tremendous market in the United States for seamless steel tubing used in the oil and gas drilling exploration industry. They will not be subject to the kinds of quota impositions which Senator Heinz's Bill would be providing.
The Bill before us today will identify where the steel is coming from and where it is going to in the United States. When we create a tonne of steel and sell it to the United States from a fabricator or processor, we get about an hour's work on a tonne of steel. When we create it from iron ore or coal we get about eight hours' work.
We may be facing this same situation on other fronts. Clearly we will if the Government's move toward a free trade agreement were to be established. Regardless of that, our largest customer for many commodities is the United States. If the U.S. Congress moves to a have a managed trade system on other commodities this kind of monitoring service may be required.
Although Algoma Steel showed a profit in the first quarter-other companies have been more profitable-I do not think anyone believes that the steel industry is out of the woods yet. In the United States in the last four or five years over 300,000 jobs have been lost in the steel industry. We have lost many in Algoma Steel. We want to look to the day when there will be an opportunity for things to pick up in the oil and gas industry and so be able to sell steel to the U.S. If this action
being taken through Bill C-57, were not taken we could not be sure when a Bill would come through the Senate or the House of Representatives to roll us back to some unreasonable percentage of our historical share of the U.S. market. The steel industry faces a long period of difficulty because of new commodities and products coming onto the market-place today.
If we are to work on a sectoral basis as we have with the Auto Pact, this can be done with steel. This industry is highly integrated. We buy American material and equipment and sell our finished product to them, and vice-versa. It is really a North American integrated industry. Percentages like Canada's 4.7 per cent of the American market send people like Senator Heinz into orbit. Often we find that the big steel manufacturing companies in the U.S. are buying semi-finished steel from Canadian companies. That kind of information will be revealed. It is very hard for the American steel industry to be complaining about Canadian imports when Americans are buying semi-finished material from our steel mills because the industry is highly integrated. There is movement back and forth.
I want to mention that the steel caucus of the House of Commons and the steel caucus in the United States made up of people in the Congress and House of Representatives have done a lot to assist in the understanding and provision of cooperation between the two countries on this issue. I hope the passage of this Bill well lead to an even greater understanding of the Canadian position so that we will not have this vital industry hampered by unreasonable protectionist methods in the United States. If it does, countries importing steel which are under voluntary restraint agreements will be affected. They will be caught by the mechanism, and the Draconian effect that protectionist methods would have on our integrated steel operations will not occur.
With those few comments, I would like to indicate my support for this legislation. I think it will be very important to the Canadian steel industry.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the third time and passed.
